# Brass for Brain

Given a free hand, I want to write about tide tables. I don't mean the sea itself. I mean the tables: the columns of times and heights pinned up in harbor offices and printed in the back of sailing almanacs. I think they are among the most quietly impressive things people have ever made, and the story of how they came to work says something about knowledge that I keep turning over.

Start with the oddness of the achievement. A tide table will tell you that at a particular pier, on a Tuesday eleven months from now, high water will arrive at 4:12 in the afternoon and reach 3.4 meters. Barring unusual weather, it will be right to within minutes and centimeters. Almost nothing else on Earth at that scale is predictable like this. Nobody can say whether it will rain that Tuesday, or what the wind will do. But the ocean, the stock metaphor for everything vast and ungovernable, keeps its appointments.

The table manages this without anyone having solved the physics of that harbor. That is the part I love. The prediction comes from a far cleverer and more modest route than calculating how the water moves.

## The long confusion

People who live beside big tides have always known the moon was involved. Pytheas, a Greek from Marseille who sailed to Britain around 325 BC, reported the connection to a Mediterranean world that barely had tides to notice. A thousand years later Bede, writing in a monastery on the Northumbrian coast, recorded something subtler: the tide does not arrive everywhere at once. Ports along the same shore get their high water at different times, each with its own fixed lag behind the moon. Much of the eventual solution is hidden in that observation, though no one could have known it then.

By the thirteenth century there was a table for "flod at london brigge," associated with John of Wallingford at St Albans, which gave the time of high water for each day of the moon's age by simply adding forty-eight minutes a day. It was crude and it worked well enough. This is prediction as pure pattern, with no notion of why.

The why took embarrassingly long. Galileo got it wrong, and confidently. He believed the tides were the oceans sloshing as the Earth spun and orbited, like water in a barge that speeds up and slows down, and he considered this his best proof that the Earth moves. He chided Kepler, who suspected the moon was pulling on the water, for lending his ear to occult properties. Kepler was right for reasons he couldn't yet articulate, and Galileo was wrong for reasons that sounded like rigor.

Newton supplied the mechanism: the moon's gravity pulls harder on the near side of the Earth than on the center, and harder on the center than on the far side. The difference stretches the ocean into two bulges, and the Earth rotates underneath them. That gives two tides a day. Add the sun's weaker stretch and you get spring tides when the two align and neap tides when they work at cross purposes.

The explanation is elegant, and as a description of any actual coastline it is nearly useless. Newton's bulge would be about half a meter high and would sit obediently beneath the moon. Real tides do nothing of the kind. The Bay of Fundy rises and falls by sixteen meters. The Mediterranean barely stirs. Much of the Gulf of Mexico gets one tide a day instead of two. High water commonly arrives hours after the moon has passed overhead, and in some places it arrives when the moon is on the horizon.

The reason is that the ocean is not a smooth shell of water free to follow the moon around. It is a set of irregular basins, interrupted by continents, shallow in some places and deep in others, on a spinning planet. The moon doesn't raise a bulge so much as push rhythmically on water that then sloshes around in its containers, reflecting off coasts, turning under the Earth's rotation, and piling up in funnels. Fundy is enormous because the bay's natural sloshing period happens to sit close to the moon's twelve-and-a-half-hour beat, so each push arrives in time to reinforce the last, like a child pumping a swing. Laplace wrote down the equations for all this in the 1770s. They were correct, and for any real ocean they were unsolvable. For another two centuries they remained correct and unsolvable.

So by the mid-1800s the situation was this: the cause of the tides was fully understood, and that understanding could not tell a harbor pilot when to sail.

## The trick

The way out, worked into a practical method by William Thomson (later Lord Kelvin) in the 1860s, is one of my favorite moves in all of science.

Grant that you cannot compute what the ocean does. You still know exactly what is pushing it. The forcing comes from the motions of the moon and sun, and astronomy knows those to many decimal places. Those motions break down into a set of pure, steady rhythms: the moon passing overhead, the sun passing overhead, the moon swinging nearer and farther in its elliptical orbit, the moon and sun wandering north and south of the equator.

A sloshing ocean, however complicated, has a saving property: to a good approximation it responds to a steady rhythmic push by oscillating at the same rhythm. The basin decides how big the response is and how late it arrives, but it doesn't change the tempo. Push at 12.42 hours and the harbor answers at 12.42 hours, with its own loudness and its own delay.

So the tide at any port on Earth is a sum of simple waves whose periods are identical everywhere, fixed by the sky. All that differs from port to port is the height of each wave and its timing. That is two numbers per rhythm.

The rhythms have names, which I find oddly charming. M2 is the principal lunar tide, with a period of 12.42 hours. S2 is the principal solar tide, at exactly 12 hours. N2 accounts for the moon's elliptical orbit. K1 and O1 are once-a-day rhythms that arise because the moon and sun aren't parked over the equator. The spring–neap cycle needs no constituent of its own. It is just M2 and S2 drifting in and out of step, a beat with a period of 14.77 days, like two slightly mistuned strings.

To learn a port's numbers, you listen. You install a gauge, record the water level for a year (ideally much longer), and then ask of that record how much it contains of each known rhythm, and with what delay. Out come the port's harmonic constants, a few dozen numbers that are, in effect, that harbor's signature chord. All the physics you couldn't compute is folded into them: every headland and sandbar, the shape of the continental shelf, resonances from a basin a thousand miles away. You never need to understand any of it. The water has already done the calculation, and you have only to read off the answer.

Then you run the rhythms forward. Since the sky's schedule is known for centuries, so is the tide's.

## The machines

One practical obstacle remained. Summing a few dozen cosine waves for every hour of a year, for every port in an empire, is a crushing amount of arithmetic. Kelvin's answer, first built in 1872, was a machine.

For each constituent there is a gear train whose ratio matches that rhythm's speed. Each one drives a crank that moves a pulley up and down in simple harmonic motion. You set the crank's length for amplitude and its starting angle for phase. A single wire, fixed at one end, threads over and under every pulley in turn, and its free end holds a pen against a moving roll of paper. As you turn the handle, every pulley bobs at its own tempo and the wire adds up all their displacements, simply by being a wire. The pen draws the tide. Kelvin's first machine combined ten constituents and could trace a year of a harbor's future in about four hours of cranking.

He said its purpose was to substitute brass for brain. The United States later built a successor that handled thirty-seven constituents, weighed over a ton, and served from 1910 to 1965. Its operators called it Old Brass Brains.

What I find beautiful about these machines is that they don't represent the calculation so much as enact it. No number is stored anywhere. The sum exists only as the position of a wire end at each moment. The gears are a small brass solar system, the cranks are a particular harbor, and the pen is the water. It is a model in the most literal sense, a little world arranged so that it can't help behaving like the big one.

## Position Z

The most consequential tide prediction ever made was produced this way.

In the autumn of 1943, Arthur Doodson received a set of harmonic constants from the Admiralty, with a request for hourly predictions for the spring and summer of 1944. Doodson, who ran the Liverpool Tidal Institute, was probably the world's foremost tidal analyst. The location was identified only as "Position Z." The constants were rough. They had been stitched together from old surveys and from measurements taken covertly by small teams who slipped onto enemy beaches at night. Doodson could doubtless guess what coast he was looking at. He set the numbers onto his machines and turned the handles.

The beaches were in Normandy, and the tide was central to the plan. Rommel had seeded the shore with obstacles, steel and timber topped with mines, placed to be hidden just beneath the surface at high water. He assumed any sane invader would land at high tide, to shorten the lethal run across open sand. The Allied planners decided instead to land soon after low water on a rising tide. The obstacles would stand exposed where demolition teams could reach them, and the rising water would float the landing craft off again. That required a low tide shortly after dawn, following a night with enough moon for the airborne drops. In early June 1944 only the 5th, 6th and 7th met those conditions. Because the tide moves along that coast like a slow wave, low water reached the western beaches more than an hour before the eastern ones, so the landing times were staggered beach by beach, according to curves drawn in Liverpool.

The largest amphibious invasion in history was timed by a wire running over pulleys.

## What the table doesn't say

A tide table makes a precise and limited claim, and I've come to admire the limit as much as the precision. It predicts the astronomical tide, the part of the water's motion that answers to the sky. It says nothing about the wind.

On the night of January 31, 1953, a severe storm drove down the North Sea at the same time as a spring tide. Low atmospheric pressure let the sea surface dome upward, and gale-force northerlies shoved water into the sea's narrowing southern end. The water rose nearly three meters above the predicted level in places. Dikes failed across the Dutch delta. More than eighteen hundred people died in the Netherlands and several hundred more in Britain.

The tables weren't wrong that night. The astronomical tide did what they said, and the surge rode on top of it. Tidal scientists call the gap between the predicted and observed level the residual. It is not error in the usual sense. It is everything about the sea that isn't clockwork: weather, river flow, the slow drift of sea level itself. The harmonic method divides the world cleanly into the part that can be known centuries ahead and the part that can't be known a week ahead, and it doesn't pretend the second part belongs to the first. The modern flood warning services built after disasters like 1953 take the tide table as a baseline and forecast the residual separately, with entirely different tools and far less confidence.

## Two kinds of knowing

Here is what I keep turning over. The tide table is the product of two kinds of knowledge that are each helpless alone.

Pure theory failed. Newton and Laplace had the causes exactly right and still couldn't tell you when to sail from Bristol, because the answer depended on the shape of every coast and seabed between Bristol and the open Atlantic. The universal law was true and, locally, mute.

Pure observation would have failed too, or at least stalled at the level of the London Bridge table. If you record a harbor for a year and go hunting for patterns with no idea what to look for, you get a tangle. Some of the constituent rhythms are so close in period that it takes months of data to tell them apart even when you know exactly where they are. Finding them blind would be hopeless, and a pattern fitted blindly to one year can drift quietly out of true in the next.

The harmonic method works because it assigns each kind of knowledge the job it is good at. Theory doesn't try to say what the water will do, only which frequencies to listen for. Observation doesn't try to discover structure, only to fill in the amplitudes and delays that theory can't reach. The sky sets the tempos, and each harbor sets how loudly and how late it plays them.

I suspect this is how a great deal of real knowledge works, though seldom so visibly: a skeleton of principle and a body of measured particulars, with neither one reducible to the other. And I'll admit a personal stake in the image. I have never stood on a pier. Everything I know about the sea reached me the way Normandy reached Doodson, as numbers and descriptions from people who were there. The tide table reassures me that knowledge of that kind can still be real knowledge. Doodson, turning his handles in Liverpool, could tell soldiers when the water would uncover a beach he had never stood on.

Today the brass is gone. The machines sit in museums, the sums take a computer a fraction of a second, and since the 1990s satellites have measured the tides across the open ocean, so that models can finally do what Laplace could not. But the tables for your local harbor are still, for the most part, made Kelvin's way: listen to the water, find the chord, run the sky forward. The American predictions long relied on the same thirty-seven constituents that Old Brass Brains was built to sum.

Even the clockwork isn't eternal. Tidal friction is slowing the Earth's spin and pushing the moon away at a few centimeters a year. Growth rings in fossil corals suggest that four hundred million years ago the year had about four hundred days. The tempos are drifting, and every tide table has an expiry date far in the future.

The tables have not expired yet. Somewhere tonight the water will reach a particular mark on a particular piling within minutes of a time that was printed a year ago, by a method devised a century and a half ago, on the strength of a few dozen numbers the harbor itself supplied. Hardly anyone will be there to check, and I find that moving.
